source.title: Pushing the Limits of High-Resolution Weather Forecasting through Data Scaling
source.authors: Yang Zhao; Pei-Song Niu; Tian Zhou; Ziqing Ma; Guanlong Ma; Rong Jin; Huiling Yuan; Liang Sun

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent cutoff or garbling affecting the reported scaling results.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests data scaling in a new forecasting domain and refines the simple power-law picture with a nonzero saturation floor, lead-time- and variable-dependent exponents, and diminishing returns. T5 takes precedence over an extension classification because these results qualify the form and scope of the scaling claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports weather-forecast RMSE scaling with training-data volume, not language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute. It does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Rows below capture its data-scaling fits, stated RMSE improvements, exponent variation, and reported saturation; weather-model comparisons unrelated to scaling are omitted.
record.test_reason: The paper fits a power law with an irreducible-error term to 0.1° weather-forecast RMSE as training-data volume (years, part SR-synthetic) grows. That is a result on whether the scaling form holds in a new modality (V5). It says nothing about language-model loss, compute allocation, shape or downstream tasks. I classify it T3 rather than T5: its saturation floor is part of the fitted form, and it argues against no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that 0.1° forecast RMSE follows power-law improvement with training-data volume, with exponents that shrink at longer lead times and a saturation floor. They also conclude that high-resolution forecasting is primarily data-bottlenecked, and that per-variable super-resolution of ERA5 is an effective way to supply that data.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales weather-forecast training-data volume and measures forecast RMSE, fitting a power law with an irreducible-error term. It does not use language-model pretraining loss or sweep model parameters, tokens, and training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponent varies with forecast lead time and meteorological variable. The paper also reports different performance for per-variable versus full-variable SR data, and cautions that gains diminish beyond 18 years.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted data-scaling exponent β varies systematically by forecast target and lead time; it decays with lead time, which the authors attribute to chaotic divergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In autoregressive forecasting, data-scaling exponents shrink as the prediction horizon lengthens.

record.problems: The scaling fits are reported without uncertainty intervals. Table 6 gives fits for four representative variables at three lead times; the paper cautions that extrapolation beyond 18 years is trend analysis, not a definitive performance estimate. The scaling models were trained for single-step prediction without rollout fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: Fig. 4 plots additional pointwise curves for data types and forecast horizons, but the flattened text does not provide their individual numerical values. Excluded those unreported point values; the fitted representative-variable results and the paper's explicit aggregate reductions are recorded above. Other forecast benchmark and weather-event results do not measure the scaling behavior targeted here.

untested.parts: No language models, no pretraining cross-entropy, no parameter or compute sweeps.
No held-out large runs predicted from small-run fits; the extrapolation beyond 18 years is unverified.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
Only data volume is scaled, over less than one order of magnitude (about 5–18 years). Model size and compute are not scaled. No image, video, repeated-data or fine-tuning regimes.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules or published laws.

missing.what: The data volumes (years) used as fit points, and how many runs, are not stated in the text, so the order-of-magnitude range of the fit can't be confirmed.
Per-variable SR data beats full-variable SR data at 10 years (Fig. 4, point 4). This shows that the quality of the added data changes where runs fall on the curve. No numbers are given.

record.verdict_notes: The fitted β values (up to 2.7) come from very few points over roughly 5–18 years, and E∞ absorbs much of the curvature. Treat the exponents as descriptive. No uncertainty is reported on the fits. The scaled data mixes real 0.1° analysis with SR-synthetic data. The architecture is fixed at 821.65M parameters, so data is the only axis scaled.

versions.untested_parts: No language models, held-out pretraining cross-entropy, or sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No language-model loss extrapolation. The paper discusses extrapolating its weather-data fits beyond 18 years but says this is trend analysis, not a definitive performance estimate.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests data-volume scaling for high-resolution weather forecasting using RMSE. It does not test image/video models or the listed repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
The forecast task is the paper's primary task, not downstream performance predicted from language-model scale or pretraining loss.

Reports weather-data scaling exponents varying by forecast lead time and variable, and a fitted saturation floor. Does not test language-model setup or fitting choices, disagreements among published language-model laws, parameter-counting, training schedules, or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: BaguanHR
rows.operation_detail: Assess fitted RMSE scaling curves beyond 18 years of training data
rows.measure: Marginal RMSE improvement with more training data
rows.baseline: Fitted trend through the 18-year data threshold
rows.value: Fitted curves suggest marginal gains gradually diminish beyond 18 years; most variables plateau early while MSL retains headroom
rows.note: Authors caution that extrapolation beyond 18 years is a trend analysis rather than a definitive performance estimate.
rows.check: This is an extrapolation of fitted curves beyond the observed data. The authors call it 'trend analysis rather than a definitive performance estimate', so it is not a measured result.

relationships.condition: 0.1° weather forecasting, data-volume scaling, 6h single-step RMSE plus 72h T2M and aggregate 72h/120h RMSE reductions
relationships.reason: Power law plus floor fits 6h RMSE with R²≥0.95 for all four variables (r1–r4) and 72h T2M with R²=0.938 (r5). Going from 7 to 18 years cuts RMSE 4.6% at 72h and 4.9% at 120h (r13, r14).
relationships.display_finding: Offset power laws fitted 6h RMSE with R²≥0.95 for all four variables and 72h T2M with R²=0.938; increasing training coverage from 7 to 18 years reduced RMSE by 4.6% at 72h and 4.9% at 120h.

relationships.condition: Longer lead times (72h U10/MSL/Z500; all 120h variables), autoregressive rollout from single-step models
relationships.reason: Fit quality drops (R² 0.69–0.87) and β falls with lead time, e.g. T2M 2.207→0.792. The power-law form holds only loosely here, over a data range under one decade (r6–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Fit R² fell to 0.69–0.87 and scaling exponents decreased with lead time, including T2M from 2.207 to 0.792, over less than one decade of data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: BaguanHR high-resolution weather forecasting, with training-data volume varied and RMSE measured
reader_labels.reason: The fitted weather RMSE curves follow a power-law form with an irreducible-error term, and expanding data from 7 to 18 years is reported to reduce RMSE at 72 and 120 hours (r1–r14).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported weather-forecast fits across the tested lead times and variables
reader_labels.reason: Fitted exponents differ across lead times and variables, and the authors report diminishing gains and saturation rather than one unbounded power law (r1–r12, r15).
